ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteology:
Why this matters: the anterior abdominal wall is a layered muscular sheet whose aponeuroses build the rectus sheath and the inguinal canal — the weak points where hernias appear. Master the nine regions, the wall layers, the rectus sheath (arcuate line) and the inguinal canal/hernias, and surface anatomy, incisions and groin lumps all make sense.
Regions & Surface Anatomy
The nine regions
  • Two vertical (midclavicular) and two horizontal planes divide the abdomen into 9 regions
  • Top: right hypochondrium · epigastrium · left hypochondrium
  • Middle: right lumbar (flank) · umbilical · left lumbar
  • Bottom: right iliac (inguinal) · hypogastrium (suprapubic) · left iliac
Key planes & landmarks
  • Transpyloric plane of Addison (L1) — midway xiphisternum→umbilicus; pylorus, fundus of gallbladder, pancreatic neck, SMA origin, hila of kidneys
  • Subcostal (L3) & transtubercular (L5) planes; the McBurney’s point (⅓ from ASIS to umbilicus) overlies the appendix base
Layers of the Anterior Abdominal Wall
Superficial → deep
  • Skin
  • Superficial fascia: Camper’s (fatty, superficial) & Scarpa’s (membranous, deep) — below the umbilicus
  • Muscles (with their investing fasciae)
  • Transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum
Scarpa’s continuity
  • Scarpa’s fascia continues into the perineum as Colles’ fascia and onto the penis/scrotum (dartos)
  • Explains how extravasated urine (ruptured spongy urethra) tracks into the scrotum & up the abdominal wall
The Muscles
MuscleFibre directionNote
External obliqueInferomedial (“hands in pockets”)Aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament
Internal obliqueSuperomedial (at right angles to EO)Contributes to the conjoint tendon
Transversus abdominisTransverse (horizontal)Deepest; contributes to the conjoint tendon
Rectus abdominisVertical (paired straps)Tendinous intersections; flexes the trunk
The three flat muscles' aponeuroses enclose rectus abdominis as the rectus sheath and fuse in the midline as the linea alba; the lateral edge of rectus abdominis is the linea semilunaris. All are innervated by the anterior rami of T7–T12 (& L1).
The Rectus Sheath & Arcuate Line
Above the arcuate line
  • The internal oblique aponeurosis splits around rectus abdominis
  • Anterior wall: external oblique + anterior lamina of internal oblique
  • Posterior wall: posterior lamina of internal oblique + transversus abdominis
Below the arcuate line
  • All three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis
  • The posterior wall is just transversalis fascia (a potential weak point)
  • The arcuate line lies ~⅓ of the way from umbilicus to pubis
The Inguinal Canal
Rings & walls
  • An oblique ~4 cm passage above the inguinal ligament; the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) → the superficial ring (a defect in the EO aponeurosis)
  • Anterior wall: EO aponeurosis (+ IO laterally)
  • Posterior wall: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially)
  • Roof: arching fibres of IO & TA · Floor: inguinal ligament (+ lacunar ligament medially)
Contents
  • The spermatic cord (♂) or the round ligament of the uterus (♀)
  • The ilioinguinal nerve (enters through the superficial ring; lies on the cord, not within it)
The inguinal ligament is the rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
The Spermatic Cord
Contents (rule of 3s)
  • 3 arteries: testicular, cremasteric, artery to the vas deferens
  • 3 nerves: genital branch of the genitofemoral (the nerve to cremaster), sympathetic fibres, & the ilioinguinal nerve (which runs on the cord, not within its coverings)
  • 3 other: vas (ductus) deferens, pampiniform plexus of veins, lymphatics
3 coverings (from 3 layers)
  • External spermatic fascia — from external oblique
  • Cremasteric fascia — from internal oblique (& the cremaster muscle)
  • Internal spermatic fascia — from transversalis fascia
Inguinal Hernias & Hesselbach’s Triangle
Hesselbach’s (inguinal) triangle
  • Medial: lateral border of rectus abdominis
  • Lateral: inferior epigastric vessels
  • Inferior: inguinal ligament
  • A direct hernia pushes through this triangle
Indirect vs direct
  • Indirect (commonest) — through the deep ring, LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis); can enter the scrotum
  • Direct — through Hesselbach’s triangle, MEDIAL to the inferior epigastric vessels; acquired (weak wall)
Reduce & occlude the deep ring. If pressure over the deep ring (just above the mid-inguinal point / the femoral pulse) controls a reduced hernia, it is indirect; a direct hernia still bulges. A hernia below & lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral; above & medial is inguinal.
The Posterior Abdominal Wall
Psoas major — from the lumbar vertebrae to the lesser trochanter (with iliacus = iliopsoas, the chief hip flexor); a psoas abscess tracks to the groin.
Quadratus lumborum — 12th rib & lumbar transverse processes to the iliac crest; laterally flexes the trunk.
Iliacus — the iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter.
The umbilical folds on the inner wall: median (urachus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries) & lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).
Clinical Correlations
Incisions — midline (through linea alba, avascular), gridiron/McBurney (appendix), Pfannenstiel (suprapubic, obstetric/pelvic), paramedian.
Rectus sheath haematoma — torn inferior epigastric vessels below the arcuate line → a painful mass mimicking an acute abdomen.
Caput medusae — dilated para-umbilical veins in portal hypertension (portosystemic anastomosis).
Divarication of recti — stretched linea alba (pregnancy) → a midline bulge on sitting up.
Referred pain — the umbilicus is the T10 dermatome (early appendicitis pain).
🧠 Mnemonics
Spermatic cord coverings — “Externally, Cremaster Internally”: External spermatic (EO), Cremasteric (IO), Internal spermatic (transversalis).
Indirect = lateral to the inferior epigastric; direct = medial (MDs don’t lie: Medial = Direct).
Rectus sheath below the arcuate line — all aponeuroses go in front.
Cord contents — 3 arteries, 3 nerves, 3 others (rule of threes).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Nine regions divided by 2 midclavicular & 2 horizontal planes; transpyloric plane = L1.
Superficial fascia below umbilicus = Camper’s (fatty) + Scarpa’s (membranous).
External oblique fibres point inferomedially (“hands in pockets”).
Below the arcuate line, all three aponeuroses lie anterior to rectus; posterior wall = transversalis fascia.
Deep ring = lateral to inferior epigastric; superficial ring = defect in EO aponeurosis.
Inguinal ligament = EO aponeurosis, ASIS → pubic tubercle.
Indirect hernia = lateral to inferior epigastric (through deep ring, congenital); direct = medial (Hesselbach’s, acquired).
Hernia below & lateral to the pubic tubercle = femoral; above & medial = inguinal.
Ilioinguinal nerve lies on the cord, not within it.
Abdominal wall innervation = T7–T12 & L1 anterior rami.
ABDOMEN__Viscera / Organs:
Why this matters: the abdominal viscera are organised by their embryological gut division — foregut, midgut & hindgut — which dictates their blood supply, nerve supply & pain referral. Add the peritoneal relations (intra- vs retroperitoneal) and the biliary tree, and appendicitis, biliary colic, bowel ischaemia and referred pain all fall into place.
The Peritoneum
Layout
  • Parietal peritoneum lines the wall (somatic pain, well localised); visceral peritoneum covers organs (autonomic, poorly localised, midline referred)
  • Greater sac & lesser sac (omental bursa), communicating through the epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow
  • Intraperitoneal organs have a mesentery; retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum
Retroperitoneal — “SAD PUCKER”
  • Suprarenals · Aorta/IVC · Duodenum (2nd–3rd) · Pancreas (except tail) · Ureters · Colon (ascending & descending) · Kidneys · Esophagus · Rectum
  • The omenta: greater omentum (“abdominal policeman”) & lesser omentum (liver → stomach/duodenum)
Foregut, Midgut & Hindgut
DivisionOrgansArteryReferred pain
ForegutOesophagus → mid-duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleenCoeliac trunk (T12)Epigastrium
MidgutMid-duodenum → proximal ⅔ transverse colonSMA (L1)Periumbilical
HindgutDistal ⅓ transverse colon → upper rectumIMA (L3)Suprapubic
The gut divisions explain appendicitis pain (early periumbilical = midgut visceral, then RIF = parietal) and why foregut pain is epigastric. The boundary is the 2nd part of the duodenum (foregut/midgut) at the major duodenal papilla.
The Stomach
Structure
  • Regions: cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum & pylorus; lesser & greater curvatures
  • The lesser omentum attaches to the lesser curvature; the greater omentum & gastrosplenic ligament to the greater curvature
Blood supply (coeliac trunk)
  • Lesser curve: left gastric (coeliac) + right gastric (hepatic)
  • Greater curve: left gastro-omental (splenic) + right gastro-omental (gastroduodenal)
  • Fundus: short gastric arteries (splenic)
The Small Intestine
Duodenum (C-shaped, 4 parts)
  • 1st (superior) — the “cap”, intraperitoneal; commonest site of duodenal ulcer
  • 2nd (descending) — receives the major duodenal papilla (of Vater) (bile + pancreatic duct)
  • 3rd (horizontal) — crossed by the SMA/SMV (SMA syndrome)
  • 4th (ascending) — ends at the duodenojejunal flexure (ligament of Treitz)
Jejunum vs ileum
  • Jejunum (upper left) — thicker wall, tall plicae circulares, long vasa recta, few arterial arcades
  • Ileum (lower right) — thinner, Peyer’s patches, short vasa recta, many arcades; ends at the ileocaecal valve
  • Meckel’s diverticulum — “rule of 2s” (2% · 2 ft from the ileocaecal valve · 2 inches long)
The Large Intestine
Features & parts
  • Identified by teniae coli, haustra, omental appendices & a wide calibre
  • Caecum & appendix (base at McBurney’s point; teniae converge on the appendix), ascending, transverse, descending & sigmoid colon
  • The appendix position is most often retrocaecal
Blood supply
  • SMA (midgut): ileocolic, right colic, middle colic → to the proximal ⅔ of the transverse colon
  • IMA (hindgut): left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal
  • The marginal artery of Drummond links SMA & IMA; the splenic flexure is a watershed (ischaemia)
Liver, Gallbladder & Biliary Tree
Liver
  • Four anatomical lobes (right, left, caudate, quadrate); functionally divided by the vessels into 8 Couinaud segments
  • The porta hepatis transmits the portal triad: portal vein, hepatic artery & (common) hepatic duct
  • Ligaments: falciform (with the ligamentum teres = obliterated umbilical vein), coronary & triangular; the bare area
Biliary tree & Calot’s triangle
  • R + L hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct + cystic duct → common bile duct → joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater (sphincter of Oddi)
  • Calot’s (cystohepatic) triangle — cystic duct, common hepatic duct & inferior liver edge; contains the cystic artery (a key landmark in cholecystectomy)
Pancreas & Spleen
Pancreas
  • Retroperitoneal (except the tail); head (in the duodenal C, with the uncinate process), neck, body & tail (to the splenic hilum, in the splenorenal ligament)
  • The main pancreatic duct joins the CBD at the ampulla; the SMA/SMV pass behind the neck
Spleen
  • Intraperitoneal, in the left hypochondrium along ribs 9–11; the largest lymphoid organ
  • Related to the stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure & tail of pancreas; supplied by the splenic artery; ruptures with left lower rib fractures
Kidneys, Ureters & Adrenals
Kidneys (retroperitoneal, T12–L3)
  • The right kidney is lower (pushed down by the liver); each has cortex, medullary pyramids → papillae → minor → major calyces → renal pelvis
  • Hilum (front→back): renal Vein, Artery, ureter (Pelvis); the left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta
  • Anterior relations differ (right: liver, duodenum, colon; left: stomach, pancreas, spleen, colon)
Ureters & adrenals
  • Ureter runs on psoas major, crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac at the pelvic brim; three constrictions (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ)
  • Adrenal (suprarenal) glands — retroperitoneal caps on each kidney; cortex (zona glomerulosa/fasciculata/reticularis) & medulla; rich 3-source arterial supply, single vein (R → IVC, L → left renal vein)
Clinical Correlations
Appendicitis — periumbilical pain (midgut visceral) migrating to McBurney’s point (parietal) with guarding.
Biliary colic / cholecystitis — RUQ pain, Murphy’s sign; gallstones may lodge at the ampulla → obstructive jaundice/pancreatitis.
Peptic ulcer — a posterior duodenal (D1) ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery → brisk haemorrhage.
Mesenteric ischaemia — SMA occlusion → “pain out of proportion”; the splenic flexure watershed is vulnerable.
Splenic rupture — left lower rib fracture → intraperitoneal haemorrhage, Kehr’s sign (left shoulder-tip pain).
Portal hypertension — portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal & rectal varices, caput medusae.
🧠 Mnemonics
Retroperitoneal — SAD PUCKER: Suprarenal, Aorta/IVC, Duodenum, Pancreas, Ureters, Colon, Kidneys, (o)Esophagus, Rectum.
Gut arteries — foregut = coeliac (T12), midgut = SMA (L1), hindgut = IMA (L3).
Renal hilum — front-to-back VAU: Vein, Artery, Ureter (“VAU”).
Meckel’s rule of 2s — 2%, 2 ft from ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 tissue types.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Foregut → coeliac/epigastric; midgut → SMA/periumbilical; hindgut → IMA/suprapubic pain.
Foregut/midgut boundary = 2nd part of duodenum (major duodenal papilla).
Portal triad in the porta hepatis: portal vein, hepatic artery, common hepatic duct.
Calot’s triangle (cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver edge) contains the cystic artery.
CBD + main pancreatic duct join at the ampulla of Vater (sphincter of Oddi).
Large bowel = teniae coli, haustra, omental appendices; teniae converge on the appendix base.
Splenic flexure = SMA/IMA watershed (ischaemic colitis).
Right kidney is lower than the left; the left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta.
Spleen lies along ribs 9–11; ruptures with left lower rib fractures (Kehr’s sign).
Gastroduodenal artery lies behind D1 — eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer.
